facts.text: Fault tree analysis (FTA) starts from an unwanted top event and works downward to identify combinations of smaller failures that could cause the event, joined by AND and OR logic.
facts.quote: A fault tree starts from one unwanted top event and works downward, drawing the combinations of smaller failures that could cause it, joined by AND and OR logic.

facts.text: A fault tree for a machine failing to brake for a person in its path can use an OR gate to represent four causes: the person is not detected, the person is detected but not judged a threat, the brake command is not sent, or the brake does not apply.
facts.quote: Beneath it an OR gate lists the ways: the person is not detected, or is detected but not judged a threat, or the brake command is not sent, or the brake does not apply.

facts.text: The booklet does not use fault trees by name.
facts.quote: The booklet does not use fault trees by name.

facts.text: The booklet's two separate safety functions—failure to intervene and unsafe or unnecessary intervention—are the closest match to fault tree analysis because they are suitable fault-tree top events.
facts.quote: The closest match is its two separate safety functions, failure to intervene and unsafe or unnecessary intervention, which are exactly the kind of top events a fault tree starts from [Chapter 3]

facts.text: The booklet warns about common-cause errors, which break the independence assumed by an AND gate in fault tree analysis.
facts.quote: its warnings about common-cause errors, which break the independence an AND gate assumes [Chapter 13].

facts.text: Fault tree analysis can reveal where a shared component, such as a single power supply or one software module, undermines the redundancy claimed by a design.
facts.quote: A fault tree makes visible where one shared part, such as a single power supply or one software module, quietly undermines the redundancy the design claims.
